what_its_for: Methylnaltrexone is used to treat constipation caused by opioid pain medicines (such as morphine, oxycodone, or hydrocodone). It works in your gut to block the constipating effects of opioids without affecting the pain relief they provide. It is used in adults who are taking opioid medicines for ongoing (chronic) non-cancer pain or for pain related to advanced illness.
how_to_take: Methylnaltrexone comes as a liquid injection given under the skin (subcutaneous injection), usually in the stomach area, upper arm, or thigh. It also comes as a tablet taken by mouth. If you are using the injection, your doctor or nurse will show you exactly how to inject it at home. Rotate injection sites each time and do not inject into skin that is sore, bruised, red, or hard. If taking the tablet form, swallow it whole with water on an empty stomach, at least 30 minutes before your first meal of the day.
dosing: The dose depends on your body weight and the form you are using. For the injection, a common adult dose is 12 mg injected under the skin once daily as needed (not more than once every 24 hours). For the tablets, the usual adult dose is 450 mg (three 150 mg tablets) taken by mouth once daily. Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your weight and kidney function. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions.
missed_dose: Take or use your missed dose as soon as you remember, as long as it has been at least 24 hours since your last dose. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and go back to your regular schedule. Do not take or inject two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store methylnaltrexone tablets at room temperature, away from heat, moisture, and light. Store the injection vials or prefilled syringes at room temperature and protect them from light. Do not freeze the injection. Once you remove a vial from the box, you can keep it at room temperature and must use it within 30 days. Discard any unused medication properly and keep all medicines out of reach of children.
what_to_avoid: Do not stop taking your opioid pain medicine without talking to your doctor first. Avoid using methylnaltrexone if you have a bowel blockage (bowel obstruction), as it may make this dangerous condition worse. Be cautious when driving or doing activities that require alertness until you know how this medicine affects you. Tell your doctor about all other medicines you take, including over-the-counter drugs and supplements, as some medicines can interact with methylnaltrexone.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you experience: severe stomach pain, cramping, or bloating that is unusual or gets worse; blood in your stool; nausea or vomiting that is severe; signs of a tear in your stomach or intestines (severe abdominal pain, fever, nausea, vomiting); opioid withdrawal symptoms such as sweating, chills, runny nose, feeling anxious, or yawning; diarrhea that is severe or does not stop; or signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, hives, swelling of the face, lips, or throat, or difficulty breathing.
when_it_works: Methylnaltrexone often works within 30 minutes to 4 hours after taking a dose. Most people have a bowel movement within this time frame. If you do not have a bowel movement after using this medicine, contact your doctor before taking another dose.
special_populations: Kidney problems: If you have severe kidney disease, your doctor will lower your dose. Liver problems: Use with caution if you have severe liver disease; tell your doctor about any liver conditions. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: It is not known if this medicine is safe during pregnancy or breastfeeding. Talk to your doctor before using it if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Children: This medicine is not approved for use in children. Elderly patients: Older adults may be more sensitive to side effects; your doctor will monitor you closely.
